blogs.title: Indefinitely Pending: Exemption 7(A) and the Problem of Open-Ended Counterterrorism Investigations
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's application of the 'pending or reasonably anticipated' standard for Exemption 7(A) in the context of a counterterrorism investigation that has spanned over two decades. It examines the tension between CREW's requirement for a 'concrete prospective law enforcement proceeding' and the court's deference to the FBI in national security cases, and asks whether the ruling effectively creates an open-ended exemption for counterterrorism files that can be invoked indefinitely so long as an investigation technically remains 'ongoing.' The post also considers the court's candid acknowledgment that the FBI's update declaration was 'surprisingly terse' in isolation, yet adequate when read against prior submissions—a reasoning move that may lower the bar for agencies seeking to maintain withholdings over long periods.

blogs.title: Behind the Screen: Ex Parte Declarations and the Structural Asymmetry of National Security FOIA Litigation
blogs.description: This post focuses on the court's treatment of ex parte declarations, which were central to both the Exemption 7(A) analysis and the segregability determination. It examines the court's candid admission that ex parte submissions 'handicap' FOIA plaintiffs but its conclusion that this is simply 'inherent' in cases where public disclosure would defeat the purpose of the exemption. The post also analyzes the waiver issue—Farahi did not oppose the government's motion to file ex parte, and the court held this precluded him from challenging reliance on those declarations—and discusses the broader implications for FOIA's transparency goals when the government's justifications are largely invisible to the requester and the public.

blogs.title: Stale Declarations and the Duty to Update: Procedural Practice in Long-Pending FOIA Cases
blogs.description: This post examines the district court's notable procedural decision to deny the FBI's initial summary judgment motion without prejudice and require updated declarations because of the 'significant passage of time' since the original submissions. It analyzes the D.C. Circuit's endorsement of this approach and its treatment of the supplemental Bender declaration as an 'update' to—rather than a standalone replacement for—the original Hardy declarations. The post discusses what this means for FOIA practice: how long is too long between agency declarations and summary judgment rulings, what standard applies to 'update' declarations versus original ones, and what obligations agencies have to maintain the currency of their exemption justifications in protracted FOIA litigation.

blogs.title: Words vs. Information: The Segregability Standard and Vast Government Records
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's segregability ruling, which affirmed the FBI's withholding of approximately 10,750 pages and 80 CDs in their entirety. It focuses on the D.C. Circuit's reliance on the Mead Data Central principle that FOIA's focus is on 'information, not simply words which the Government has written down,' and the corollary that individually disclosable words scattered throughout a document may not be 'reasonably segregable.' The post examines the tension between FOIA's statutory mandate to release 'any reasonably segregable portion' and the practical reality of reviewing enormous volumes of records, and discusses whether the 'inextricably intertwined' standard functions as a practical safe harbor for agencies dealing with massive files.
